s: Las lies ten stades from the sea and forty from Gythium, between the mountains Ilium, Asia, and Cnacadium. Its sights include temples of Athene, Carnean Apollo, Dionysus, and Æsculapius, and it contains the tomb and statue of its founder Las.

l: Sparta, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Sparta was the authority over Cardamyle after Emperor Augustus detached Cardamyle from Messenia. The people of Leuctra worshipped Carnean Apollo in the same way as the people of Sparta.

l: Achilles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Achilles was said by the people of Las to have killed Las when he came to ask Tyndareus for Helen in marriage, but Pausanias states that Patroclus killed Las. The text argues from Homer that Achilles was not bound by Tyndareus’ oath and was not represented as one of Helen’s suitors.

l: Patroclus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Patroclus is identified as the person who killed Las, contrary to the local tradition that attributed the killing to Achilles. The text says that Patroclus, rather than Achilles, wooed Helen.

l: Helen, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Helen was the woman whom the local tradition said Achilles sought to marry from Tyndareus. The text argues that Achilles could hardly have been one of her suitors, citing Homer’s account of Achilles’ relation to the sons of Atreus and the age of Theseus.

l: Homer, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Homer is cited for saying that Achilles went to Troy to gratify the sons of Atreus and was not bound by an oath to Tyndareus. He is also cited for describing Achilles’ descent from Hades traditions without naming Cerberus, and for mentioning Cardamyle and Enope.

l: Pyrrhus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, was said to have given the river Scyras its name after landing there with his fleet on the way from Scyrus to marry Hermione. He was also associated with the naming of Pyrrhichus, and the daughters of Nereus were said to have climbed to Cardamyle to see him depart for Sparta.

l: Pyrrhichus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Pyrrhichus lies about forty stades inland from the river Scyras. It was said to have been named either after Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, or after the god of the Curetes, and it also had traditions connecting it with Silenus; its temples included those of Artemis and Apollo Amazonius.

l: Tænarum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Tænarum is a promontory with the harbours Achilleus and Psamathus, a cave-like temple of Poseidon, and works of art including a statue of Arion riding a dolphin. It also had a fountain once believed to reveal harbours and ships, though its power ended after a woman washed dirty linen in it; Cænepolis was formerly called Tænarum.

l: Cerberus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Cerberus was traditionally described as the dog that Hercules brought up from the lower world through the cave at Tænarum. Hecatæus instead said that Cerberus was a deadly serpent reared at Tænarum, while the text notes that Homer did not give the underworld dog this name or a complete description.

l: Thalamæ, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Thalamæ lies about eighty stades by road from Œtylus and has a temple and oracle of Ino where answers are received through dreams. The temple also contains statues of Pasiphae and the Sun, and a sacred spring called the water of the Moon.

l: Pephnos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Pephnos lies by the sea about twenty stades from Thalamæ and has a small island of the same name in front of it. The people of Thalamæ say that Castor and Pollux were born there, and the island contains small bronze statues of them that remain unmoved despite winter waves.

l: Leuctra, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Leuctra lies about twenty stades from Pephnos, though the reason for its name is unknown. It contains temples or statues of Æsculapius, Ino, Cassandra, Carnean Apollo, Athene, and Eros; a statue of Ithomatan Zeus was discovered there after a fire cleared part of a wood.

l: Cardamyle, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Cardamyle is the city Homer called Cardamyle in Agamemnon’s promises of gifts. It is subject to Sparta after Emperor Augustus detached it from Messenia, lies eight stades from the sea, and contains a grove sacred to the daughters of Nereus and temples of Athene and Carnean Apollo.

l: Gerenia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Gerenia is the city formerly called Enope by Homer and is inhabited by Messenians who join the council of the Eleutherolacones. Some said Nestor was brought up there, while others said he fled there after Hercules took Pylos; Gerenia contains the tomb and temple of Machaon.

l: Nestor, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Nestor was said by some to have been brought up in Gerenia, while another tradition said that he fled there after Hercules took Pylos. The text also says that Nestor recovered the bones of Machaon.

l: Machaon, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Machaon, the son of Æsculapius, has a tomb and temple in Gerenia, where his sacred place is called Rhodon and his bronze statue stands upright. The Little Iliad says that Eurypylus killed him, and the tradition says that Nestor recovered his bones.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The unit describes the origins, rulers, religious traditions, and early history of Messenia, including its settlement by Polycaon and Messene and the establishment of Andania. It traces the succession from Perieres, Aphareus, and Neleus through the Dorian takeover under Cresphontes and the restoration of Æpytus. It recounts the disputes between the Messenians and Lacedæmonians, especially the cases of Teleclus, Polychares, and Euæphnus. The conflict became open war when the Lacedæmonians captured Amphea under Alcamenes during the reign of Euphaes.

l: Messenia, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Messenia was originally described as uninhabited and was named after Messene, the wife of Polycaon. Its rulers, cities, religious institutions, and conflicts with the Lacedæmonians are traced from its earliest traditions through the capture of Amphea.

l: Laconia, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Laconia was formerly called Lelegia under Lelex, and its border with Messenia was fixed at Gerenia by Augustus. Polycaon and Messene gathered an army from Laconia and Argos to invade the country that became Messenia.

l: Polycaon, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Polycaon, the younger son of Lelex, married the Argive Messene and became a ruler of the country later called Messenia. He and Messene established their royal headquarters at Andania, but later traditions criticized their neglect of Zeus on Ithome.

l: Messene, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Messene was the proud Argive daughter of Triopas and wife of Polycaon. She helped invade and name Messenia, lived with Polycaon at Andania, and was said to have established games for the Great Goddesses.

l: Andania, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Andania was the royal headquarters of Polycaon and Messene and was the place where the mysteries of the Great Goddesses were celebrated in ancient times. Lycus introduced the mysteries there to Aphareus, his sons, and Arene.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The Lacedæmonians participated in the settlement of Messenia, later disputed traditions concerning Teleclus and the sanctuary of Artemis Limnas, and went to war against Messenia. They secretly prepared for war, swore not to abandon it until Messenia was won, and captured Amphea under Alcamenes.

l: Ithome, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Ithome was associated with Messenia, and the later city of Messene was built near it. A sacred enclosure of Zeus stood on its summit, though it had been neglected by Polycaon and Messene until Glaucus restored its worship.

l: Great Goddesses, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: The rites and mysteries of the Great Goddesses were introduced into Messenia by Caucon from Eleusis and later taught by Lycus to Aphareus, his family, and Arene. The mysteries were celebrated at Andania, and annual rites there continued in the time of Sybotas.

l: Perieres, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Perieres, the son of Æolus, became king after the descendants of Polycaon had died out. He received Melaneus at his court and had by Gorgophone the sons Aphareus and Leucippus.

l: Aphareus, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Aphareus succeeded Perieres as king with his brother Leucippus and held the greater power. He built Arene, received Neleus, and learned the mysteries of the Great Goddesses from Lycus.

l: Arene, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Arene was built by Aphareus and named after the daughter of Œbalus, who was his wife and uterine sister. Aphareus and his sons lived there, and Lycus came there after fleeing from Athens.

l: Neleus, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Neleus, the son of Cretheus, fled from Pelias at Iolcus and was received into Aphareus’ house. Aphareus gave him the maritime parts of Messenia, including Pylos, where Neleus established his seat of government.

l: Pylos, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: Pylos was among the maritime cities given by Aphareus to Neleus, who made it his seat of government. During the reign of Nestor and his descendants, the royal court was located there.

l: Nestor, Description of Greece, BOOK IV.--MESSENIA.
s: After the deaths of the sons of Aphareus, the kingdom of Messenia devolved upon Nestor, the son of Neleus. His descendants were later driven from Messenia by the Dorians and the return of the Heraclidæ.
